text: The Tasmanian tiger, properly called the thylacine, was a striped hunter that once lived across Australia and New Guinea. It disappeared from the mainland about 3,000 years ago and survived only on the island of Tasmania. There, after Europeans arrived, it was hunted, trapped and poisoned. The last known thylacine died in Hobart Zoo on 7 September 1936.

Since then, people have reported thousands of sightings, but none has been proven with a clear photo, body or DNA. Scientists consider the thylacine [[extinct|extinct]]. Some are now trying to bring it back.

sec.h: Not a tiger, not a dog
sec.t:
A thylacine was about the size of a medium dog, with a stiff tail and between 13 and 21 dark stripes across its back. Those stripes gave it the nickname "tiger". Its head looked so much like a wolf's that even experts can mix up the skulls.

But it was a [[marsupial|marsupial]], related to kangaroos and koalas. Females raised their babies in a pouch. It could open its jaws extremely wide, and it sometimes stood up on its back legs and tail, like a [[@wild-kangaroo|kangaroo]]. Thylacines and wolves ended up looking alike because they did the same job: chasing and catching prey.

Aboriginal rock paintings in northern Australia show thylacines, some painted thousands of years ago. Then, around 3,000 years ago, they vanished from mainland [[@australia|Australia]]. Scientists think a mix of causes was to blame: a drier [[climate|climate]], growing human populations, and the arrival of the dingo, a wild dog that competed for the same food. Dingoes never reached Tasmania, which may be why thylacines lasted there.

{{story:extinction-today}}

When European settlers brought sheep to Tasmania in the 1800s, farmers blamed thylacines for killing them, though wild dogs and poor farming were often the real cause. From 1888 to 1909, the Tasmanian government paid a reward, called a bounty, for every thylacine killed. It paid out 2,184 times, and private companies paid more.

Disease, dogs and the clearing of forests added to the pressure. By the 1920s thylacines were rare. Tasmania made them a protected [[species|species]] in July 1936, and the last known animal died in the zoo two months later. Short black-and-white films of it pacing in its cage are the only moving pictures we have.

The last known thylacine lived at Beaumaris Zoo in Hobart. It's often called Benjamin, but historians say that name appeared decades later, and there's no record of keepers using it. On some cold nights in 1936 it was reportedly locked out of its shelter, and it died on 7 September.

In 1933 a naturalist named David Fleay filmed it for about a minute. The clip shows it pacing, sniffing and opening its jaws in a huge yawn. Since 1996, Australia has marked 7 September as National Threatened Species Day, in its memory.

Every year people report seeing a thylacine in the Tasmanian bush. Searches with cameras have found nothing certain. A 2023 study of sighting records suggested a few might have survived into the late 1900s, though other scientists doubt it.

Meanwhile, in 2022 a company working with the University of Melbourne announced a plan to recreate the thylacine. It wants to use DNA from museum specimens and the cells of a living relative, the fat-tailed dunnart. Whether that would really bring back a thylacine is a question at the heart of [[@lost-de-extinction|de-extinction]]. And the thylacine wasn't the only animal hunted away within living memory. In America, the continent's most common bird went the same way, as the story of the [[@lost-passenger-pigeon|passenger pigeon]] shows.

text: Stegosaurus had two rows of tall, flat plates along its back. They were thin and covered in grooves for blood vessels, so they probably weren't good armour. Most scientists think they were for display: to look bigger, to recognise their own kind, and to show off to mates.
Its tail had four long spikes. Those were real weapons. A [[fossil|fossil]] Allosaurus has a hole in a tail bone that fits a Stegosaurus spike.

sec.t:
The plates were made of bone with a spongy inside and a thin outer layer. They were not fixed to the backbone. Instead, they sat in the thick skin, standing up in two staggered rows.

From the side, they made the animal look much taller, a bit like a [[@peacock-tail|peacock's tail]] makes a peacock look bigger. The plates may have been brightly coloured, too, though colour is rarely kept in fossils. Some scientists once thought the plates helped warm up in the sun or cool down in the breeze, because of all those blood vessels. That idea is still discussed, but display is the most common view.

In 1982, the American cartoonist Gary Larson drew a Far Side [[@comics-art|cartoon]] of a caveman teacher pointing at a Stegosaurus tail. He named the spikes after "the late Thag Simmons". Of course, no human ever met a Stegosaurus.

Scientists enjoyed the joke so much they began using "thagomizer" in talks and papers. It is now a common nickname. The spikes were serious, though. Swung by a strong tail, they could hit hard enough to break bone, as the injured Allosaurus shows. The spikes pointed out to the sides and slightly up, so a swing swept them through the air like a club.

Its brain was small for its body, no bigger than a lime, in an animal nearly as long as a school bus. Yet [[@dino-brains|dinosaur brains]] can't be judged by size alone. Stegosaurus and its relatives lasted for millions of years, which suggests they were well suited to their lives.

Its head was low and narrow, with small, leaf-shaped teeth. It probably ate ferns, cycads and other low plants, perhaps rearing up on its back legs sometimes to reach higher.

The most complete Stegosaurus skeleton known is nicknamed Sophie. She was found in Wyoming and is now in the [[@dino-museums|Natural History Museum]] in London. Scientists used her to work out how heavy Stegosaurus was: about the weight of a rhinoceros.

T. rex lived about 66 million years ago. Stegosaurus lived about 150 million years ago. So more time separates them than separates T. rex from you. "Dinosaur times" were not one moment. They were [[@dino-age-span|165 million years long]].

text: The Western Ghats are a long chain of hills and mountains that runs for about 1,600 km along India's west coast, from Gujarat down to the southern tip at Kanyakumari. They are not very tall by world standards, but they matter enormously.

They catch the southwest [[@monsoon|monsoon]], so their slopes are among the wettest places in India. That rain feeds great rivers like the Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri, which carry water across southern India to farms and cities. The forests are also packed with plants and animals that live nowhere else.

In 2012, UNESCO named the Western Ghats a World Heritage Site. Scientists list them as one of the world's top hotspots of [[biodiversity|biodiversity]], meaning a place unusually rich in different kinds of life.

st.reveal: Moist winds from the Arabian Sea rise over the hills, cool and drop their rain on the western slopes. By the time the air sinks down the other side, much of its water is gone. This drier zone is called a rain shadow.

myth: The Western Ghats are young mountains, like the Himalayas.

They are far older. The Himalayas began rising about 50 million years ago, while the edge of the Western Ghats formed much earlier, as India broke away from Madagascar and the land was later shaped by erosion.

sec.h: A wall that catches the rain
sec.t:
Every June, moist winds blow in from the Arabian Sea. When they reach the Ghats, they are forced upwards. The air cools, its water vapour turns to clouds, and rain pours down on the western slopes.

Towns like Agumbe in [[@karnataka|Karnataka]] can get several metres of rain a year. Then the air spills over the top and sinks down the eastern side, now much drier. That is why [[@pune|Pune]] is drier than Mumbai, and Bengaluru gets far less rain than coastal Mangaluru.

The rain doesn't stay in the hills. The Godavari begins near Nashik and the Kaveri at Talakaveri in Kodagu. Both rise close to the west coast, yet flow east across the whole [[peninsula|peninsula]] into the Bay of Bengal.

{{story:frogs-monsoon}}

Long isolation and steady rain have given the Ghats a huge number of [[endemic|endemic]] [[species|species]], ones that live in this region and nowhere else. The [[@wild-lion-tailed-macaque|lion-tailed macaque]], a black monkey with a silver mane, swings through the [[canopy|canopy]]. The Nilgiri tahr, a wild goat, clings to grassy cliffs near Munnar in [[@kerala|Kerala]]. The [[@king-cobra|king cobra]], the world's longest venomous snake, hunts other snakes in the leaf litter.

New species are still being found. In 2003, scientists described the purple frog, a bloated, pig-nosed creature that lives underground and comes up only to breed when the [[monsoon|monsoon]] arrives. Its closest relatives live in the Seychelles, a clue that India and those islands were once joined.

On the hills of the Nilgiris, a shrub called neelakurinji flowers only once every 12 years, turning whole slopes blue-purple.

The Western Ghats are not young, folded mountains. Their steep western edge is the broken rim of a continent. When India split from [[@madagascar|Madagascar]], roughly 90 million years ago, the edge of the land was left as a step, and erosion has been carving it ever since. [[@india-drift|India's long drift]] north left this cliff facing the sea.

In the north, around Mahabaleshwar, the hills are built from layers of dark lava called [[basalt|basalt]]. These came from the giant eruptions that made the [[@deccan|Deccan Traps]] about 66 million years ago, around the time the dinosaurs died out.

Around 2011, a panel of experts led by the ecologist Madhav Gadgil recommended strong protection for large parts of the Ghats. Many villagers, farmers and state governments argued that the rules would harm jobs and development. A later committee proposed protecting a smaller area. People still disagree about how to balance forests, farms, mines and roads, and the debate continues in all six states the hills cross.

என்ன தவறு நடந்தது என்று இஸ்ரோ பொறியாளர்கள் ஒவ்வொரு விவரத்தையும் அலசினார்கள். சந்திரயான்-3-க்காக விக்ரமுக்கு வலுவான கால்கள், கூடுதல் எரிபொருள், கூடுதல் [[sensor|உணரிகள்]], இன்னும் பெரிய இலக்கு எல்லாம் கொடுத்தார்கள். ஒரு சிறிய புள்ளியைக் குறிவைப்பதற்குப் பதிலாக, சுமார் 4 கி.மீ. நீளமும் 2.4 கி.மீ. அகலமும் கொண்ட ஒரு பகுதியில் எங்கே வேண்டுமானாலும் அது இறங்கலாம். யோசனை எளிமையானது. தவறுகள் நடக்கும் என்று எதிர்பார்த்தே திட்டமிடு, நடந்தாலும் தாக்குப்பிடி.

சுமார் 30 கி.மீ. உயரத்திலிருந்து விக்ரம் தன் கடைசி இறக்கத்தைத் தொடங்கியது. அப்போது அதன் வேகம் மணிக்குச் சுமார் 6,000 கி.மீ. துப்பாக்கிக் குண்டை விட வேகம். சுமார் 20 நிமிடங்கள் அதன் இன்ஜின்கள் எரிந்து வேகத்தைக் குறைத்தன. பூமியிலிருந்து நிலவுக்கு ரேடியோ சிக்னல் போய்ச் சேரவே ஒரு நொடிக்கு மேல் ஆகும். கட்டளைக்காகக் காத்திருக்க நேரமில்லை. அதனால் விக்ரம் தானாகவே பறந்தது. அதன் கேமராக்களும் உணரிகளும் தரையை அலசின. சுமார் 150 மீ. உயரத்தில் ஒரு கணம் அந்தரத்தில் நின்று, சமதளமான, பாதுகாப்பான இடத்தைத் தேர்ந்தெடுத்தது. பிறகு தன் நான்கு கால்களில் மெதுவாக இறங்கியது.

{{story:robots}}

பிரக்யான் நொடிக்குச் சுமார் 1 செ.மீ. வேகத்தில் ஊர்ந்து, மொத்தம் சுமார் 100 மீ. பயணம் செய்தது. அதன் கருவிகளில் ஒன்று மண்ணின் மீது லேசர் ஒளியைப் பாய்ச்சி, திருப்பி மின்னிய ஒளியை ஆராய்ந்தது. தென் துருவத்தருகே கந்தகம் இருப்பதை அது உறுதி செய்தது. கூடவே அலுமினியம், கால்சியம், இரும்பு உள்ளிட்ட வேறு பல [[element|தனிமங்களும்]] இருந்தன.

விக்ரமில் இருந்த ஒரு கருவி, சுமார் 10 செ.மீ. ஆழத்துக்கு ஒரு கம்பியைத் தரைக்குள் இறக்கியது. வெயிலில் மேற்பரப்பு சுமார் 70 °C இருந்தது. ஆனால் சில சென்டிமீட்டர் கீழே போனால் வெகு குளிர். நிலவின் புழுதி ஒரு நல்ல கம்பளிப் போர்வை போல வேலை செய்கிறது.

கடைசிக் கட்டத்தில், இஸ்ரோ விக்ரமின் இன்ஜின்களை இன்னொரு முறை இயக்கியது. அது சுமார் 40 செ.மீ. மேலே எழும்பி, பக்கவாட்டில் நகர்ந்து, மீண்டும் இறங்கியது. [[@apollo-moon|அப்பல்லோ விண்வெளி வீரர்கள்]] செய்தது போல நிலவுப் பாறைகளைப் பூமிக்குக் கொண்டுவரக்கூடிய எதிர்காலப் பயணங்களுக்கான ஒத்திகைதான் அந்தச் சின்னத் தாவல்.

நிலவின் துருவங்களுக்கு அருகே, சூரியன் எப்போதும் அடிவானத்தில் தாழ்வாகவே இருக்கும். அங்குள்ள சில ஆழமான [[crater|பள்ளங்கள்]] பல நூறு கோடி ஆண்டுகளாக நிழலிலேயே கிடக்கின்றன. அவற்றில் வெப்பநிலை −200 °C-க்கும் கீழே. அவற்றுக்குள் உறைந்த நீர் இருக்கலாம் என்று விஞ்ஞானிகள் நினைக்கிறார்கள். அந்தப் பனியை உருக்கிச் சுத்தம் செய்தால், ஒருநாள் விண்வெளி வீரர்களுக்குக் குடிநீர், சுவாசிக்க ஆக்சிஜன், [[@rockets-how|ராக்கெட்டுகளுக்கு]] எரிபொருள் எல்லாம் கிடைக்கலாம்.

இந்தியாவின் முதல் நிலவுப் பயணமான சந்திரயான்-1, 2008-இல் ஏவப்பட்டது. அது சுமந்து சென்ற நாசாவின் ஒரு கருவி, நிலவின் மேற்பரப்பில் நீர் மூலக்கூறுகளைக் கண்டறிய உதவியது. [[@moon-formed|நிலவு எங்கிருந்து வந்தது]] என்பது பற்றியும் அந்தப் பனி ஏதாவது சொல்லக்கூடும்.

நிலவில் ஒரு பகல் சுமார் இரண்டு பூமி வாரங்கள் நீடிக்கும். அதைத் தொடர்ந்து இரண்டு வாரம் உறைய வைக்கும் இரவு. விக்ரமும் பிரக்யானும் [[@what-if-live-on-moon|ஒரு நிலவுப் பகல்]] மட்டும் வேலை செய்யும்படி உருவாக்கப்பட்டவை. இரவு வந்ததும் இஸ்ரோ அவற்றை உறக்க நிலைக்கு மாற்றியது. அவை மீண்டும் கண் விழிக்கவே இல்லை. ஆனால் அதற்குள் தங்கள் வேலையை முடித்துவிட்டிருந்தன.

ஆகஸ்ட் 23-ஐ இந்தியா இப்போது தேசிய விண்வெளி தினமாகக் கொண்டாடுகிறது. லேண்டர் இறங்கிய இடத்துக்கு ‘சிவசக்தி முனை’ என்று பெயர். இந்தியாவின் விண்வெளித் திட்டத்தைத் தொடங்கி வைத்த விஞ்ஞானி [[@vikram-sarabhai|விக்ரம் சாராபாயின்]] நினைவாகத்தான் லேண்டருக்கு விக்ரம் என்று பெயர் சூட்டினார்கள்.

text: A spacesuit keeps an astronaut alive where a human body cannot survive on its own. In space there is no air to breathe and no air pressure to hold the body's fluids in place. Temperatures swing from hotter than [[@boiling-water|boiling]] water in sunlight to far colder than Antarctica in shadow. Tiny specks of dust and rock whizz past faster than bullets.

So a spacesuit does many jobs at once. It holds air at a steady pressure around the body and supplies fresh oxygen. It removes the [[carbon-dioxide|carbon dioxide]] you breathe out. It keeps you at a comfortable temperature, protects against dust, glare and some [[radiation|radiation]], and carries a radio so you can talk to your crew.

st.prompt: On the first spacewalk in 1965, Alexei Leonov's suit puffed up so much he couldn't fit back through the hatch. What did he do?

options.t: Let some air out of his suit
Waited for the suit to cool and shrink
Asked his crewmate to pull him in

st.reveal: Leonov opened a valve and let out some of the air, which made the suit softer and easier to bend. It was risky, because too little pressure could have made him ill. He squeezed in head first and got home safely.

d.try: Put on a pair of thick winter gloves or rubber kitchen gloves and try to pick up a coin, button a shirt or tie a shoelace. Time yourself, then try without gloves. Spacesuit gloves are stiffer still, and astronauts work in them for six or seven hours at a time.
myth: Without a spacesuit in space, your body would explode at once.

Nobody explodes. Without air pressure, a person would pass out within about 15 seconds and need help very quickly to survive. A spacesuit's main job is to stop that by keeping the body under pressure with air to breathe.

from about +120°C in sunlight to −150°C in shadow

sec.t:
Astronauts actually use two kinds of suit. During launch and landing they wear a lighter pressure suit, in case the cabin springs a leak. These are the orange or white suits you see when astronauts wave on the way to the rocket.

For spacewalks they need something much tougher. NASA's spacewalk suit has many layers, from a cooling layer next to the skin to a tough, white outer shell. Together with its backpack it weighs over 120 kg on Earth. In [[orbit|orbit]] it weighs nothing, but it is still heavy to move around, like pushing a loaded shopping trolley.

Strangely, the hard problem is often getting rid of heat, not keeping warm. An astronaut working hard makes lots of body heat, and the suit is sealed. So next to the skin astronauts wear long underwear threaded with about 90 m of thin tubes. Cool water flows through them and carries the heat away, a bit like the radiator in a car.

Inside the suit the air pressure is only about one-third of normal, which makes the suit less stiff. Before going out, astronauts breathe pure oxygen for hours to flush nitrogen out of their blood, which prevents a painful condition divers call the bends.

The suits that Apollo astronauts wore on the Moon were made by a company called ILC, part of the firm that made Playtex underwear. Skilled seamstresses stitched each suit by hand, from about 21 layers of fabric and rubber, sewing so precisely that a stitch out of place could cause a leak.

Moon dust caused trouble too. It is sharp, like tiny bits of broken glass, and it wore through layers of the suits during the Apollo missions. Engineers designing new suits for NASA's return to the Moon are working hard on that problem.

India is building its own suits for [[@gaganyaan|Gaganyaan]] astronauts. Like every spacesuit before them, they will need to fit each astronaut closely, because long hours in a badly fitting suit can leave [[@space-body|hands and shoulders]] sore and bruised.

text: The ocean covers about 71% of Earth, and its average depth is about 3.7 km. That is about 50 Qutub Minars, or about nine Empire State Buildings, stacked on top of each other. Its deepest point, in the [[@ocean-deepest|Challenger Deep]], is about 11 km down.

Scientists divide the ocean into layers, like floors in a very tall building. Sunlight only reaches the top 200 metres or so. Below 1,000 m it is completely dark. And for every 10 metres you go down, the water [[pressure|pressure]] rises by the weight of the whole [[atmosphere|atmosphere]] pressing on you at the beach.
Each layer has its own kind of life, and many deep-sea animals make their own light.

quiz.prompt: As you sink deeper into the sea, which colour of sunlight disappears first?

options.t: Blue
Red
Green

quiz.reveal: Water soaks up red light within the first few metres, so a red fish looks dark grey a little way down. Blue light reaches deepest, which is why the sea looks blue and why many deep-sea animals are red. In the dark, red is as good as invisible.

d.try: Put a red, a yellow and a blue crayon side by side. Look at them through a sheet of blue cellophane or a blue plastic folder. The red one looks almost black. Deep in the sea, where only blue light is left, red animals hide the same way.
myth: The sea is blue because it reflects the sky.
Water itself is very slightly blue. It soaks up red light and lets blue light bounce around, so deep, clear water looks blue even under a grey sky.

sec.t:
From 200 m to 1,000 m is the twilight zone. A little blue light leaks down, but not enough for plants. Animals here often have huge eyes, silvery sides or glowing bellies.

Every night, a vast crowd of shrimps, jellies and small fish swims up from these depths to feed near the surface, then sinks back down before dawn. It is probably the biggest journey made by animals anywhere on Earth, and it happens every single day.

Below 1,000 m lies the midnight zone. No sunlight reaches it at all. The water is near freezing. Here the only lights come from animals like the [[@anglerfish|anglerfish]], and sperm whales dive down to hunt [[@giant-squid|giant squid]] in the darkness.

Below 4,000 m comes the abyss, a huge, flat plain of soft mud. It covers more of Earth than all the land put together. Below 6,000 m, in a few deep cracks called trenches, lies the deepest zone of all.

Deep-sea animals have soft, watery bodies without air spaces, so the huge pressure doesn't crush them. Many eat "marine snow": bits of dead [[plankton|plankton]] and droppings drifting down from above. When a whale dies and its body sinks to the floor, it can feed crowds of creatures for decades.

In 1977, scientists in the US submersible Alvin explored the seabed near the [[@galapagos|Galápagos Islands]]. They found [[@geysers-hot-springs|hot springs]] gushing from cracks in the ocean floor, called hydrothermal vents. Around them lived giant tube worms, clams and crabs.

These animals don't depend on sunlight at all. [[bacteria|Bacteria]] at the vents make food from chemicals in the hot water, and the worms and clams live off the bacteria.

Most of the deep sea has still never been seen. Only about a quarter of the seabed has been mapped in detail. Robot [[@submarines|submarines]] and India's planned crewed submersible, [[@ocean-exploration-india|Matsya-6000]], keep searching, and new animals turn up on almost every trip.

text: Inside a toilet cistern is a float, a hollow ball or plastic cup that bobs on top of the water. It is joined to the valve that lets water in from the pipe. When you flush, the cistern empties, the float drops and the valve opens. Water rushes in. As the water rises, the float rises with it. When the water reaches the right level, the float pushes the valve closed, and the hissing stops.

There is no electricity, no [[sensor|sensor]] and no chip. The cistern uses [[buoyancy|buoyancy]], the upward push of water on things that float, and a simple [[lever|lever]]. Just in case the valve fails, an overflow pipe carries extra water safely away.

st.prompt: If a cistern's float got stuck at the bottom, what would happen?

options.t: Water would keep running and spill into the overflow pipe
The tank would never fill at all
The toilet would flush over and over by itself

st.reveal: The float is what tells the valve to close. If it can't rise, the valve stays open and water keeps pouring in. That is why cisterns have an overflow pipe, so extra water drains away safely instead of flooding the bathroom.

Tie a small piece of sponge or a bottle cap to a pencil laid across the cup's rim like a see-saw, with the other end over the straw. Lower the cup into a bowl of water and watch the float rise and press on the straw.
myth: Thomas Crapper invented the flushing toilet.

Thomas Crapper was a real plumber in London in the late 1800s, and he sold toilets and patented some improvements. But flushing toilets existed long before him. Alexander Cumming patented the S-bend in 1775, and John Harington built a flushing toilet in the 1590s.
facts: a float valve, often called a ball cock or fill valve

an overflow pipe that carries extra water away

sec.t:
In older cisterns, you can see a plastic or copper ball on the end of a long metal arm. This is called a ball cock. The arm is a [[@lever-lift|lever]]. The ball sits on the long end, and the valve on the short end.

Because of the lever, a small upward push from the float becomes a strong push on the valve, enough to hold back water at mains pressure. Newer cisterns use a tall plastic tube with a float that slides up and down it, but the idea is the same.

You can adjust the water level by bending the arm or turning a screw. A lower level saves water with every flush.

sec.h: The bend that blocks the smell
sec.t:
In 1775, a London watchmaker named Alexander Cumming patented the S-bend, a curved pipe under the toilet that always holds a little water. That water plugs the pipe, so sewer gases can't come up. Every toilet, sink and drain today still uses a version of his idea.

Even earlier, in the 1590s, an English courtier named John Harington built a flushing toilet for Queen Elizabeth I. It didn't catch on. People needed piped water and sewers first, and those came hundreds of years later.

sec.h: Half a flush or a full one
sec.t:
Many modern toilets have two buttons. The smaller one releases about 3 litres, the bigger one about 6. This dual flush system was developed in Australia around 1980, during a time of water shortages. Older toilets used as much as 9 to 12 litres every flush.

In India, the Bureau of Indian Standards sets rules for cistern sizes, and many new buildings use dual flush to save water. In dry cities like Chennai, every litre matters.

Look inside a rooftop water tank in an Indian house, and you may find the same floating valve, stopping the pump's water from overflowing. Farm water troughs use it to refill for cattle. The carburettors of older cars and scooters used a tiny float too, to keep just the right amount of petrol ready for the engine.

Floating works because of a rule the Greek thinker Archimedes figured out more than 2,000 years ago, which also explains how huge [[@floating-ships|steel ships stay afloat]]. And the toilet itself has an even longer story, going back thousands of years to the [[@oddity-ancient-toilets|ancient toilets]] of Mohenjo-daro and Rome.

text: In an open pot, water can't get hotter than its [[@boiling-water|boiling]] point, which is about 100°C at sea level. Any extra heat just turns more water into steam, and the steam drifts away.

A pressure cooker has a lid that locks on and a rubber ring, called a gasket, that seals the gap. When the water boils, the steam can't escape. It builds up and squeezes everything inside, raising the pressure. Under higher pressure, water must get hotter before it boils, about 120°C in a typical cooker. Food cooked at 120°C instead of 100°C softens much faster. Rajma that might take more than an hour in an open pot can be ready in well under half that time.

st.prompt: In an open pot at sea level, water boils at 100°C. Inside a sealed pressure cooker, what happens to the boiling point?

options.t: It rises to about 120°C
It stays at 100°C
It drops to about 80°C

d.try: Get a plastic medicine syringe with no needle from a chemist or first-aid kit. Pull the plunger halfway out, press your fingertip firmly over the open end, and push the plunger in. Feel the trapped air pushing back. That push is pressure, the same thing that builds up inside a sealed cooker.
myth: Pressure cookers can easily explode.

Modern cookers have several layers of safety, including the whistle, a backup safety valve or plug, and a lid that won't open while pressure is high. Accidents are rare and usually happen when a vent is blocked with food or someone forces the lid open too early.
facts: about 1 bar, so roughly double normal air pressure

sec.t:
On top of the lid sits a small metal weight over a narrow pipe. While the pressure is low, the weight sits snugly and blocks the pipe. As steam builds up, it eventually pushes hard enough to lift the weight. A jet of steam rushes out with a [[@whistles|loud whistle]], the pressure drops a little, and the weight drops back down.

So the whistle is really a pressure limiter. It keeps the inside of the cooker at roughly the same high pressure the whole time. In millions of Indian kitchens, cooks count whistles as a kind of timer: two whistles for rice, perhaps five for chana. They aren't measuring pressure, just how long the food has been cooking hot.

Indian cooking relies heavily on [[@pulses-dal|dal]], beans, chickpeas and rice, all of which need a long time in hot water. A pressure cooker saves time and fuel, which matters when [[@cooking-gas|gas cylinders]] cost money. Companies such as Hawkins and Prestige have sold cookers in India for decades, and in many families a cooker is one of the first things bought for a new home.

Cookers are popular in the USA too, often as electric "multi-cookers" with buttons instead of whistles. These use the same idea, just with a [[sensor|sensor]] and a chip deciding when the pressure is right. When cooking is done, the pressure has to come down before the lid can open. Many cooks simply wait for the cooker to cool, so the steam slowly turns back into water and the pressure falls on its own.

Cookers matter most where the air is thin. In Leh, in [[@ladakh|Ladakh]], water in an open pot boils at about 88°C. Potatoes and rice stay hard for a long time, and some foods never cook properly. A pressure cooker raises the pressure back up, so the water can get hot enough again.

Mountaineers on Himalayan [[expedition|expeditions]] carry small cookers for the same reason. [[@people-army-life|Soldiers posted]] at [[@altitude|high altitude]] along India's northern borders use them every day. Without the trapped steam, a simple bowl of hot dal would be very hard to make.

text: A Bollywood song is made by a team. The film's director explains the moment in the story: a wedding, a break-up, a chase in the rain. The music director [[@behind-theme-music|composes a tune]]. A lyricist writes the words. Arrangers add instruments, and playback singers record the song in a studio.

Only then is the song filmed. On set, the recording plays through loudspeakers while actors dance and move their lips to match. This is called lip-syncing. That is why [[@pop-cartoon-voices|the voice you hear]] and the face you see usually belong to different people, and why great playback singers became as famous as the stars.

st.reveal: Songs are usually recorded first by professional playback singers. On set, the recording is played through loudspeakers and actors move their lips to match it.

sec.t:
India's first talking film, *Alam Ara*, came out in 1931 and already had seven songs. The actors sang live as they were filmed, with musicians hiding off camera. One film made the next year, *Indrasabha*, is said to have had around seventy songs.

[[@singing|Singing live]] was hard. Actors had to be good singers as well as good actors, and every mistake meant filming again. In the mid-1930s, studios began recording songs separately and playing them back during filming. Playback singing changed everything. Actors no longer needed to sing, and the best voices in India could be heard on screen.

From the 1940s to the 1990s, a small group of singers recorded thousands of songs. [[@lata-mangeshkar|Lata Mangeshkar]] and her sister Asha Bhosle sang for heroines. Mohammed Rafi, Kishore Kumar and Mukesh sang for heroes.

Fans could recognise these voices in a single line. Music directors such as S.D. Burman, his son R.D. Burman, and the duo Shankar–Jaikishan became household names. Poets like Sahir Ludhianvi and Gulzar wrote lyrics that people still quote.

sec.h: A radio station across the sea
sec.t:
In the 1950s, India's national broadcaster, [[@radio-india|All India Radio]], cut back on film songs, which some officials saw as too light. Listeners turned elsewhere.

Radio Ceylon, from Colombo in [[@sri-lanka|Sri Lanka]], began playing Hindi film songs, and its countdown show *Binaca Geetmala*, hosted by Ameen Sayani from 1952, became hugely popular across India. Families gathered around radios to hear which song was number one. All India Radio later started its own film music service, Vividh Bharati, in 1957.

From the 1990s, [[@film-music-composers|composers]] like [[@ar-rahman|A.R. Rahman]] brought digital recording, [[@electronic-music|electronic sounds]] and global styles into film music. In 2009, his song *Jai Ho*, with words by Gulzar, won an Academy Award.

Today, songs are often released online before a film comes out, to build excitement. Many become hits at weddings and parties, and in Indian communities from Toronto to Texas. A good song can outlive the film it was made for by decades.

text: Ustad Bismillah Khan was a master of the shehnai, a wind instrument that sounds a little like a bright, singing oboe. He was born in 1916 in Dumraon, in Bihar, into a family of court musicians. As a boy he moved to [[@varanasi|Varanasi]] to learn from his uncle, Ali Bux, who played at the Kashi Vishwanath temple.

Before him, the shehnai was mostly heard at [[@life-weddings-world|weddings]] and temple gates. Bismillah Khan took it onto the concert stage and made it a classical instrument. In 2001 he was given the Bharat Ratna, India's highest civilian award.

options.t: At weddings and temple gates
Only in royal battles
Only in film studios

st.reveal: The shehnai was thought of as a sound of good luck, played at weddings, festivals and the entrances of temples and palaces. Bismillah Khan helped turn it into a classical concert instrument.

myth: The shehnai is only a wedding instrument, not real classical music.
That was a common view before Bismillah Khan. He played full ragas on it at major concerts and festivals around the world, and became one of only a few musicians ever given the Bharat Ratna.

sec.h: A small pipe with a big voice
sec.t:
A shehnai is a wooden tube about the length of a school ruler or a bit more, with finger holes and a flared metal bell at the end. The player blows through a double reed: two thin strips of leaf or cane that buzz against each other.

It is a hard instrument to play softly or smoothly. Players must control their breath very carefully, and many use a trick called circular breathing, breathing in through the nose while pushing air out of the mouth. Bismillah Khan could make it bend and slide between notes almost like a human voice singing a [[@raga-time|raga]].

Shehnai players often perform with a partner who holds one steady note on a second shehnai, called the *sur*. This drone gives the main player a fixed point to weave around. It works rather like the tanpura behind a singer in [[@carnatic-hindustani|Hindustani music]], the classical style of North India.

Bismillah Khan practised for hours on the ghats, the stone steps leading down to [[@rivers-himalaya|the Ganga]]. He was a devout Shia Muslim who prayed five times a day. He also played at the Kashi Vishwanath temple and spoke with love about Saraswati, the Hindu goddess of music and learning. For him, music was a kind of prayer that belonged to everyone.

He travelled the world, playing at festivals in Europe, North America and beyond. Yet he refused to move away from Varanasi. He lived simply, in an old house in a narrow lane, surrounded by a large family he supported. He often said that nowhere else had the Ganga, and that his music came from the city.

He also played for a few films. His shehnai can be heard in the Hindi film *Goonj Uthi Shehnai* (1959), and he played for the Kannada film *Sanaadi Appanna* (1977). The documentary maker Goutam Ghose later made a film about his life.

Bismillah Khan died in 2006, at the age of 90. He was buried in Varanasi with a shehnai beside him. Today young players learn from his recordings, and his name is given to a national award for young artists from the Sangeet Natak Akademi.

The shehnai still plays at countless [[@weddings-india|weddings]]. But thanks to him, it also has a place in serious concert halls, where a single pipe of wood and metal can hold an audience completely still.

text: A culture is the shared way of life of a group of people: their languages, food, clothes, festivals, beliefs and everyday habits. Respecting a culture means treating those ways as worth understanding, even when they are not yours.

In practice it is mostly small things. You learn how to say someone's name properly. You ask before you touch a sacred object. You try a dish before deciding you don't like it. You notice when a joke depends on a stereotype, a lazy idea that everyone in a group is the same. None of this means you must agree with everything or give up your own ways. It means starting from curiosity instead of judgement.

st.reveal: Taking things with both hands shows you value the gift and the person. In Japan, people often wait to open a present later. The same both-hands habit shows respect in Korea and in many Indian homes when taking something from an elder.

n.certNote: Most people agree that curiosity and courtesy help. People disagree about where respect for a custom should stop, for example when a tradition clashes with someone's rights.

d.try: Interview a classmate, neighbour or relative who grew up somewhere different from you. Ask how they greet elders, what they eat on a special day, and one thing that surprised them about your town. Write down one custom of theirs you had never heard of.

India has hundreds of languages and many food, dress and festival traditions. The USA mixes the customs of Native nations and of families from almost every country. Two people with the same passport can grow up with very different habits.

sec.t:
Teachers often compare culture to an iceberg. Above the water are things you can see: dances, clothes, food, festivals. Below the surface, much bigger, are things you can't see. How close do people stand when they talk? Is it polite to say no directly? Is being five minutes late rude or normal?

Most misunderstandings happen below the waterline. In many American classrooms, a child who looks the teacher in the eye seems honest and alert. In parts of India, East Asia and Africa, children are often taught to lower their eyes when an elder speaks to them, as a sign of respect. The same action sends opposite messages. Neither child is being rude.

sec.h: Why we judge without meaning to

sec.t:
Names come first. Getting a name right, whether it is Nguyen, Siobhan or Venkataraghavan, tells someone you see them. If you aren't sure, just ask. A few words in someone's language help too: a "vanakkam", a "gracias" or a "shukriya" often brings a smile.

Food is another easy door. Many families in India eat with their right hand, and many in China, Japan and Korea use chopsticks. Trying the local way, and asking how, is usually welcome. Places of worship have their own rules, such as covering your head in a gurdwara or taking off your shoes in a temple or mosque. People rarely mind a visitor who asks first.

Body language matters as well. A side-to-side tilt of the head, common in south India, can mean "yes" or "I'm listening". Visitors who expect a nod often find it confusing at first.

Cultures have always borrowed from each other. Chillies came to India from the Americas, and [[@yoga-science|yoga]] is now practised in American parks. Borrowing is how food, music and words spread around the world.

People do argue about where borrowing becomes disrespect. A sacred headdress worn as a party costume upsets many Native Americans, because in their nations it must be earned. Some say any sharing is good. Others say it matters who is sharing and whether the original culture is credited.

Schools increasingly try to make room for many traditions. In 2023, New York City added [[@diwali-lights|Diwali]] to its public school holidays, alongside holidays like Lunar New Year and Eid. Children who learn about each other's festivals, food and [[@languages-world|languages]] often find the strangest customs make sense once someone explains them.

text: Every time you fold paper in half, its thickness doubles. A sheet about 0.1 mm thick becomes 0.2 mm, then 0.4 mm, then 0.8 mm. At first nothing much seems to happen. But doubling speeds up like a rolling snowball.

After 42 folds, the stack would be about 440,000 km thick, more than the 384,400 km between Earth and the Moon. The catch is that you can't really do it. Paper gets too thick, too small and too stiff to fold long before then. It's a thought experiment, a way of showing just how powerful doubling is.

st.prompt: If paper is 0.1 mm thick, how many times would you have to fold it in half to reach the Moon?

options.t: About 42
About 1,000
About a million

st.reveal: Each fold doubles the thickness. After 42 doublings, 0.1 mm becomes about 440,000 km, more than the 384,400 km to the Moon. Doubling grows shockingly fast.

d.try: Take a sheet of A4 paper and fold it in half as many times as you can. Most people stop at 6 or 7. Then try a large sheet of thin newspaper or tissue paper. Count the layers after each fold, which go 2, 4, 8, 16 and so on.
myth: Nobody can fold a sheet of paper in half more than seven times.
With an ordinary sheet, seven is about the limit. But in 2002 a high-school student folded a very long strip 12 times, and in 2011 a school team managed 13 using a giant roll of toilet paper.

sec.t:
Here is the journey, using 0.1 mm paper, with a few landmarks along the way.

After 7 folds, the stack is about 1.3 cm thick, as thick as a small notebook. After 10 folds, it is about 10 cm, the height of a coffee mug. At 17 folds, it reaches about 13 m, as tall as a four-storey building.

At 23 folds, it is about 840 m, taller than the Burj Khalifa in Dubai. At 27 folds, about 13 km, higher than planes fly and higher than Everest. At 30 folds, it passes 100 km and enters space. At 42, it reaches the Moon. And at 51 folds, it would pass the Sun, about 150 million km away.

For years, people said you could not fold paper more than seven or eight times. In 2002, Britney Gallivan, a high-school student in California, decided to test it. She worked out a mathematical formula showing how much paper each fold uses up, because the curved edge of each fold eats into the length.

Her answer: to fold 12 times in one direction, she needed a strip of paper more than a kilometre long. She got one, and walked up and down a shopping centre folding it, until she had 12 folds. In 2011, students at a school in Massachusetts used a giant roll of toilet paper and managed 13.

Each fold halves the area of the paper as it doubles the thickness. After 10 folds, a sheet the size of a cricket field would be folded into a stack the size of a large rug, 1,024 layers thick. Long before 42 folds, the stack would be a tall, thin tower too stiff to bend. Each new fold also needs much more force, because you are bending twice as many layers as before.

You would also need a sheet of paper so big it is impossible. To reach 42 folds, the original sheet would need to be enormous, far larger than any country.

Folding matters outside puzzles. Engineers use [[@origami-maths|origami]], the art of paper folding, to pack solar panels, satellite antennae and even the mirror of the James Webb Space Telescope into rockets. Once in space, they unfold to full size. And the Moon you would reach with 42 folds has been visited for real: between 1969 and 1972, twelve astronauts walked on it during NASA's [[@apollo-moon|Apollo]] missions.

text: The 60 comes from Babylon, in what is now Iraq. Babylonian [[astronomer|astronomers]] did their maths in base 60, the way we do ours in base 10. When they divided a circle or an hour into smaller parts, they used sixtieths.

Later Greek astronomers borrowed this. They split each degree of a circle into 60 small parts, and each of those into 60 smaller parts again. In Latin these were the *pars minuta prima*, "first small part", and *pars minuta secunda*, "second small part". That is where the words minute and second come from.
The [[@clocks-maths|24 hours]] in a [[@day-night|day]] came from [[@ancient-egypt|ancient Egypt]], which split daytime and night-time into 12 parts each.

st.prompt: Why is 60 such a handy number for dividing time?

options.t: It can be split evenly in lots of ways
It is the number of days in two months
It is the biggest number with two digits

st.reveal: Sixty can be divided evenly by 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20 and 30. That makes halves, thirds, quarters and sixths of an hour all whole numbers of minutes. Ten can only be divided evenly by 1, 2 and 5.

d.try: On a sunny day, push a stick upright into a pot of soil or sand, outdoors where you are allowed to be. Every hour, mark the tip of its shadow with a pebble. By the end of the day you have made a simple sundial, the kind of clock people used for thousands of years.
myth: A day is always exactly 24 hours long.

Twenty-four hours is the average length of a day measured by the Sun. The Earth's spin wobbles very slightly and is gradually slowing over millions of years, so scientists sometimes add a "leap second" to keep clocks in step.

sec.t:
Nobody knows for sure why the Babylonians chose 60. One good guess is that it divides so neatly. Sixty can be split into halves, thirds, quarters, fifths, sixths, tenths and twelfths, all without [[@fractions|fractions]]. For people doing sums by hand, that was a big help.

Some historians think it may have come from counting on your fingers. Using your thumb to count the three sections of each finger on one hand gives 12. Counting each 12 on the five fingers of the other hand gives 60.

Ancient India had its own way of dividing the day. A day and night together contained 60 *ghatis*, so each ghati was 24 of our minutes. A ghati was split into 60 *palas*, each 24 seconds long. Some astrologers and almanacs in India still use ghatis. A *muhurta*, used to choose a good time for weddings and ceremonies, is two ghatis, or 48 minutes.

In the 1720s and 1730s, Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II built giant stone [[observatory|observatories]] called [[@jantar-mantar|Jantar Mantar]] in [[@jaipur|Jaipur]], Delhi and other cities. The huge sundial in Jaipur, called the Samrat Yantra, casts a shadow that moves several centimetres a minute, so the time can be read to within a few seconds. The Jaipur observatory is now a [[@unesco-sites|UNESCO World Heritage Site]].

After the [[@french-revolution|French Revolution]], the new government wanted everything in tens. In 1793, it declared that a day would have 10 hours, each hour 100 minutes, and each minute 100 seconds. Clockmakers made special clock faces.

People hated it. They had to replace all their clocks and learn a new way of reading them. In 1795 the rule was dropped. The metric system for length and weight survived, but time stayed in sixties.

For centuries, the second was simply 1/86,400 of a day. But the Earth's spin is not perfectly steady. So in 1967, scientists redefined the second using [[atom|atoms]] of caesium, which give off waves at a very exact rate. One second is now 9,192,631,770 of those waves.

Atomic clocks are so precise they would lose less than a second in millions of years. They keep the internet, mobile phones and satellite [[navigation|navigation]] running in step.

text: India celebrates Independence Day on 15 August, the day in 1947 when British rule ended. The USA celebrates on 4 July, the day in 1776 when its Congress approved the [[@usa-wonder-philadelphia|Declaration of Independence]] from Britain. Both countries broke away from the same [[empire|empire]], 171 years apart.

The celebrations look different. In India, the Prime Minister raises the flag at the [[@red-fort|Red Fort]] in Delhi and gives a speech, schools hold flag ceremonies, and the sky fills with kites. In the USA, people hold [[@parades|parades]], family barbecues and picnics, and end the day watching fireworks. India also has a second great national day, Republic Day, on 26 January.

st.prompt: On 15 August, India's Prime Minister raises the flag at the Red Fort. On 26 January, the President opens the flag at Kartavya Path. Why the difference?

options.t: Independence Day marks rising to freedom; Republic Day marks the Constitution taking effect
The Red Fort flagpole is too tall for the President
The two ceremonies use different flags

st.reveal: On Independence Day, the flag is pulled up from the bottom of the pole, recalling the country rising to freedom. On Republic Day, the folded flag is already at the top and is unfurled, because India was already free when the Constitution came into force.

sec.t:
India became independent at midnight between 14 and 15 August 1947. In the [[@constituent-assembly|Constituent Assembly]] in New Delhi, Jawaharlal [[@nehru|Nehru]] gave his speech beginning "Long years ago we made a tryst with destiny". It was a day of joy, but also of great sorrow, because the [[@partition|Partition]] of [[@pakistan-history|India and Pakistan]] forced millions from their homes.

The next morning, 16 August, Nehru raised the flag at the Red Fort. Every year since, the Prime Minister has done the same there on 15 August. After the flag goes up, the national anthem is sung, a 21-gun salute is fired, and the Prime Minister speaks to the country.

India's Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950, making India a [[republic|republic]], a country led by elected representatives with no king or queen. That date was chosen because on 26 January 1930, the Indian National Congress had declared the goal of full independence, "Purna Swaraj".

Republic Day brings a [[@republic-day-parade|grand parade]] in New Delhi along Kartavya Path, the avenue once called Rajpath. Soldiers march, aircraft fly past, and decorated floats from each state roll by. The President takes the salute. Three days later, the Beating Retreat ceremony, with military bands, closes the celebrations.

In 1776, the 13 American colonies were in the middle of the [[@american-revolution|American Revolution]] against Britain. On 2 July, the Continental Congress voted for independence, and on 4 July it approved the Declaration, mostly written by [[@thomas-jefferson|Thomas Jefferson]]. It said that "all men are created equal", words people have argued over and fought for ever since.

The first anniversary in 1777, in Philadelphia, already had fireworks and bells. Today, Americans hang flags, march in parades, hold picnics, and watch fireworks shows over cities and lakes. In New York City, a famous [[@burgers-hotdogs|hot-dog]] eating contest takes place on Coney Island.

John Adams and Thomas Jefferson both helped create the Declaration. Later, both became President. They were rivals in politics but became friends again in old age, writing long letters to each other.

Both men died on 4 July 1826, exactly 50 years after the Declaration was approved, a few hours apart. Adams's last words were reported to be "Thomas Jefferson survives". He did not know that Jefferson had died a few hours earlier.

text: Every computer, from a phone to a supercomputer, is built from a huge number of tiny switches. Each switch is either on or off, and switches can control other switches. Group them the right way and you get parts that can add numbers, remember things and follow instructions.

Some video games give players switches too. In Minecraft, a material called redstone carries power like a wire, and torches, [[@lever-lift|levers]] and repeaters act as switches. By connecting thousands of them, players have built working [[@calculators|calculators]], memory and simple computers inside the game. They are slow and enormous, but they work on the same ideas as the chip in your phone.

st.prompt: A Minecraft lamp is wired so it lights up only when BOTH of two levers are switched on. What kind of logic gate is that?

options.t: An AND gate
An OR gate
A NOT gate

st.reveal: An AND gate gives "on" only when both inputs are on. An OR gate would light the lamp if either lever were on, and a NOT gate flips a single input, turning on into off. Real computer chips are built from billions of tiny gates like these.

myth: You need special computer parts to build a computer.

Any system with reliable on-off switches that can control other switches can, in principle, be a computer. People have built adding machines from dominoes and marbles, and whole computers out of redstone, though they are very slow.

sec.t:
The basic building blocks of a computer are logic gates. Each takes one or two on-off inputs and gives one output.

A NOT gate flips its input: on becomes off. An AND gate turns on only if both inputs are on. An OR gate turns on if either is. That's about all there is. Yet combine enough of these simple gates, and you can do any calculation a computer can do. Inside real chips, the switches are tiny [[transistor|transistors]], billions of them packed onto a [[@chips-silicon|silicon chip]] smaller than a fingernail.

A full computer needs more than an adder. It needs memory to store numbers and a clock that ticks to keep everything in step. It also needs a control unit that reads instructions one after another and tells the other parts what to do.

Minecraft builders have made all of these. Their computers can stretch for hundreds of blocks in each direction, like a city of wires. Redstone signals move slowly, so a redstone computer might do a few simple steps every second, while your phone does billions.

In 2022 a player shared a huge redstone computer that could run a tiny, low-detail version of Minecraft, a game running inside a computer built inside the same game. It was so slow that the video had to be sped up enormously to show it working.

In 1936 the British mathematician [[@alan-turing|Alan Turing]] described an imaginary machine that could carry out any calculation, given enough time and memory. Any system that can do what his machine does is called "Turing complete".

Minecraft's redstone is Turing complete. So is a simple grid game called the Game of Life, invented by the mathematician John Conway in 1970, where people have built computers out of patterns of dots. Even some card games have been shown to be Turing complete.

Building a computer out of blocks is a slow, patient way to learn how real computers work, because you can walk around inside your machine and see every wire. Many engineers say games like this first got them interested in [[@programming|programming]] and electronics.

Minecraft's education edition now includes coding lessons where students write programs to control the game. It has become one of the best-selling video games ever, and a surprising number of its players have quietly taught themselves computer science along the way.

text: A smartphone is a small, powerful computer with a phone, camera and many [[sensor|sensors]] packed inside a slim case.

Behind the screen sits a [[circuit|circuit]] board holding the main chip, which contains the processor, graphics unit and more. Memory chips hold apps and photos. Several antennas send and receive radio signals for calls, [[@wifi|Wi-Fi]], [[@bluetooth|Bluetooth]] and satellite [[navigation|navigation]]. Cameras, microphones and speakers are fitted in tiny gaps. Most of the space is taken by a flat battery.
Put together, it's a pocket-sized combination of devices that once filled a whole desk, or a whole room.

st.reveal: Phones contain an accelerometer, a chip with microscopic parts that shift slightly as the phone moves or tilts. It senses which way gravity pulls, so the phone knows which way is down and turns the screen to match.

That advice comes from older kinds of batteries. Modern lithium-ion batteries don't need to be fully emptied, and often last longer if kept away from very low and very high charge.

sec.t:
The main chip in a phone is called a system-on-a-chip, because it combines many parts that once needed separate chips. It includes the processor that runs apps, a graphics unit for games and videos, and often a special unit for [[@ai-what|artificial intelligence]] tasks like recognising faces in photos.

These chips contain billions of [[transistor|transistors]], each so small that thousands would fit across the width of a human hair. Making them takes some of the most precise factories on Earth.

The [[@apollo-moon|Apollo 11 guidance computer]], which helped land astronauts on the Moon in 1969, had only a tiny fraction of a modern phone's memory and speed.

The screen is a sandwich of layers: tough glass, a [[@touchscreens|touch-sensing layer]], and a display made of millions of tiny coloured dots. Many phones use OLED displays, where each dot makes its own light.

Most phones now have several cameras, each with a different lens for wide, zoomed or close-up shots. Software combines their pictures.

The battery is lithium-ion, the same kind used in laptops and [[@electric-cars|electric cars]]. It stores energy by moving charged lithium [[atom|atoms]], called ions, between two layers.

A phone contains several dozen chemical [[element|elements]]. Silicon makes the chips. Lithium and cobalt go into the battery. Copper wires carry electricity. Tiny amounts of [[@gold-where|gold]] coat connectors because gold doesn't rust. Rare earth elements help make speakers, [[vibration|vibration]] motors and screen colours.

Many of these materials are mined in just a few countries, sometimes in difficult or unsafe conditions. That is one reason people encourage repairing phones and [[@e-waste|recycling old ones]], so those metals can be recovered.

The IBM Simon of 1994 is often called the first smartphone, with a touchscreen and simple apps. The iPhone, launched in 2007, and [[@open-source|phones running Android]], launched in 2008, made smartphones popular across the world.

India now has hundreds of millions of smartphone users, more than any country except China. Cheap phones and low-cost [[@mobile-networks|mobile data]] brought many families online for the first time, for video calls, online classes and payments. A device that was rare when your parents were children is now, for many people, the main way they reach the internet.

text: The British were not the only Europeans who came to India to trade and stayed to rule. The Portuguese arrived first, in 1498. The Dutch, the Danes and the French followed in the 1600s. Each set up trading companies, built forts along the coast and fought both Indian rulers and each other.

In the end, the British [[@east-india-company|East India Company]] won most of these contests. But small pockets of other European rule lasted a long time. The French held Puducherry until 1954, and the [[@portuguese-india|Portuguese stayed in Goa]] until 1961.

st.reveal: The Danish East India Company set up at Tranquebar, now Tharangambadi, in 1620. Denmark kept it until 1845, when it sold the town to the British. Fort Dansborg, the Danish fort, still stands on the beach.

d.try: Find a map of India and mark these towns with small stickers or dots, using one colour for each country. Portugal had Goa and Diu, the Netherlands had Kochi and Pulicat, Denmark had Tranquebar and Serampore, and France had Puducherry and Chandernagore. Notice how many are on the coast or on a big river, and think about why.
myth: The British were the only Europeans who ruled any part of India.
The Portuguese, Dutch, Danes and French all held towns and forts in India. The French kept Puducherry until 1954, and Portugal held Goa until 1961.

sec.t:
Why did they all come? Money. Europe wanted pepper, cardamom, cinnamon and, above all, Indian cotton cloth, which was cheap, light and beautifully dyed. Whoever controlled that trade could become very rich. Ships took about six months to sail from Europe round Africa to India, so a single cargo had to be worth the risk of storms, disease and pirates. Companies sold shares to pay for the voyages, an idea that helped create modern stock markets.

The Dutch East India Company, founded in 1602, was the most powerful trading company in the world for much of the 1600s. It mostly wanted the spice islands of what is now Indonesia, but it also took over Portuguese forts in India. In 1663 the Dutch captured Kochi, and they had trading posts at Pulicat, Nagapattinam, Chinsurah in Bengal and elsewhere.

Denmark, a small country in northern Europe, set up a trading town at Tranquebar, now called Tharangambadi, on the Tamil Nadu coast in 1620. The Danes also held Serampore near Kolkata.

Tranquebar became a centre of printing and learning. Danish-backed missionaries printed books in Tamil there in the early 1700s. In 1845, Denmark sold its Indian towns to the British. Fort Dansborg still stands by the sea in Tharangambadi, and its rooms are now a small museum.

The French East India Company was founded in 1664 and made Pondicherry, now Puducherry, its main base from 1674. Its most ambitious governor, Joseph François Dupleix, wanted France to rule large parts of South India. In the 1740s and 1750s, the French and British fought a series of wars in the Carnatic region, each backing rival Indian princes.

The British won. The French lost the Battle of Wandiwash in 1760, and after that they were left with a handful of small towns: Puducherry, Karaikal, Mahe, Yanam and Chandernagore. These stayed French for almost two hundred years.

After 1947, India asked France and Portugal to hand back their [[territory|territories]]. The people of Chandernagore voted to join India in 1949. The other French towns came under Indian control in 1954, and France formally signed them over by [[treaty|treaty]] in 1962. Portugal refused to leave Goa, Daman and Diu, and in 1961 the Indian Army moved in.

You can still see the traces. [[@puducherry|Puducherry]] has French street names and a French school. Kochi has Dutch-era buildings, and Tharangambadi has its Danish fort. Each is a reminder that the story of Europeans in India had more than one player.

text: The Maratha [[empire|empire]] began with [[@shivaji|Shivaji]], a chief from the hills near Pune who carved out a kingdom in the 1600s and was crowned Chhatrapati, or emperor, in 1674. His soldiers used speed, surprise and a chain of mountain forts to wear down much larger Mughal armies.

After Shivaji, the Marathas survived a long war with the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb. Then, in the 1700s, their chief ministers, the Peshwas, pushed north and east. By the 1750s, Maratha power stretched from Tamil Nadu to Punjab and from Gujarat to Odisha. A great defeat at Panipat in 1761, and later wars with the British, brought it to an end in 1818.

st.prompt: After Aurangzeb executed the Maratha king Sambhaji in 1689, who led much of the Maratha resistance for years?

st.reveal: After Rajaram died in 1700, his widow Tarabai ruled in the name of her young son. She led the fight against Aurangzeb's armies until his death in 1707, and the Mughals failed to crush the Marathas.

d.try: Make a model hill fort from a pile of sand, soil or modelling clay. Add a winding path to the top and a wall around it. Then try "attacking" with a toy car and think about why the narrow, twisting paths made Maratha forts so hard to capture.
myth: The Marathas were a single kingdom ruled from one throne.
By the mid-1700s they were a confederacy. The Peshwa in Pune led, but great families such as the Scindias, Holkars, Gaekwads and Bhonsles ruled their own large territories.

sec.t:
The Sahyadri mountains, part of the [[@western-ghats|Western Ghats]], are steep and cut by deep valleys. Shivaji turned this landscape into a weapon. He captured and built dozens of forts on hilltops, linked by narrow paths that only locals knew well.

Maratha soldiers rode small, hardy horses and carried light weapons. They avoided big pitched battles. Instead they raided supply lines, struck at night and vanished into the hills. Shivaji also [[@kanhoji-angre|built a navy]] and sea forts such as Sindhudurg, on an island off the Konkan coast, to defend against the Siddis, the Portuguese and the British.

Under Shivaji's grandson Shahu, real power passed to his chief minister, the Peshwa. The Peshwa Bajirao I, who led from 1720 to 1740, was a brilliant cavalry general. In 1737 his army reached the outskirts of Delhi.

The Marathas collected taxes called *chauth*, a quarter of the revenue, from lands they did not rule directly, in return for leaving them alone. The Peshwas made [[@pune|Pune]] their capital and built the Shaniwar Wada palace there. Great Maratha families ruled large regions: the Scindias from Gwalior, the Holkars from Indore, the Gaekwads from Baroda and the Bhonsles from Nagpur.

One of the most admired Maratha rulers was Ahilyabai Holkar, who governed the Holkar lands from Maheshwar between 1767 and 1795. She was known for fair justice and careful government.

She paid for temples, wells, rest houses and river steps across India, from the Himalaya to the far south. In 1780 she built the present Kashi Vishwanath temple in [[@varanasi|Varanasi]]. The handloom [[weaving|weaving]] she supported at Maheshwar still produces the famous Maheshwari saris.

In 1761 a huge Maratha army met the Afghan ruler Ahmad Shah Durrani at Panipat, north of Delhi. The Marathas were badly defeated, with enormous losses. It took them a decade to recover.

They did recover, and for a time controlled the Mughal emperor in Delhi. But rivalries between the great families weakened them. The British [[@east-india-company|East India Company]] fought three wars with the Marathas, and after the last, in 1818, the Peshwa's rule ended. Many Maratha princes, such as the Scindias and Gaekwads, kept their states under British protection. In 2025, twelve forts, from Raigad to Gingee, became a [[@unesco-sites|World Heritage Site]] as the Maratha Military Landscapes of India.

text: Ancient people wrote on walls a lot, and much of it sounds very familiar. They scratched their names and the date. They left jokes, love notes, insults and drawings of gladiators. They advertised shows and backed candidates in elections. Travellers carved "I was here" on famous monuments, just as some tourists still do.
These scribbles are a gift to historians. Official carvings tell us what kings wanted remembered. [[@street-art|Graffiti]] tells us what ordinary people were thinking on an ordinary Tuesday.

st.reveal: Romans had a sense of humour about their own scribbling. The joke was written in Latin in several places, including the theatre and the basilica, where crowds gathered.

sec.h: Pompeii, the wall of the people
sec.t:
When Mount Vesuvius buried [[@pompeii|Pompeii]] in AD 79, it also preserved its walls. More than 10,000 [[inscription|inscriptions]] have been found there. Most are scratched into plaster with something sharp, or painted.

One reads, in Latin, "Gaius Pumidius Dipilus was here", with a date that works out to 3 October 78 BC. Painted notices backed candidates for town jobs, a bit like posters before an Indian election. Someone wrote a price list. Someone else practised the alphabet, letter by letter. Others drew gladiators, boats and animals.

Some messages are too rude to print. Others are sweet: lovers wrote each other's names, and one person simply greeted a friend by name. Near the snack bars where Romans bought [[@oddity-ancient-fast-food|hot food]], customers complained about the wine.

sec.h: Soldiers who signed a pharaoh's leg

sec.t:
Hagia Sophia in [[@istanbul|Istanbul]] was one of the grandest buildings in the [[medieval|medieval]] world. Up on a marble balcony, someone carved letters in runes, the alphabet of the [[@vikings|Vikings]]. Experts think it says "Halfdan carved these runes", and they date it to around the 9th century. Many Vikings worked as guards for the emperor in what was then Constantinople. Perhaps Halfdan got bored during a long ceremony.

Vikings left scribbles in other places too. In the 1100s, a group of them broke into Maeshowe, a 5,000-year-old stone tomb in the Orkney Islands of Scotland. They carved around 30 messages in runes on its walls. Some boast about treasure, some show off who was best at carving runes, and one is a drawing of a dragon-like beast.

In [[@sri-lanka|Sri Lanka]], a palace once stood on top of Sigiriya, a rock nearly 200 m high. Along the path up runs a wall that was once polished so smooth that people could see their reflection in it.

Visitors loved it so much that, roughly between the 8th and 10th centuries, they wrote around 1,800 short poems and comments on its surface. Many describe the beautiful women painted on the rock above. Some are in an early form of the Sinhala language, so the wall helps scholars study how it changed. Today visitors are banned from writing on the Mirror Wall. Guards watch the path, and anyone caught scratching a name can be fined or even jailed.

Graffiti was often illegal in the past too, and many people disliked it. Today, carving into ancient monuments is banned almost everywhere, and it can damage things that have lasted for thousands of years. Some modern street art, painted with an owner's permission, is now protected and even sold for huge sums. Whether the secret paintings of [[@banksy|Banksy]] count as art or vandalism is still argued about, which is exactly what Romans grumbled about too.

text: Rani Lakshmibai was the queen of Jhansi, a small kingdom in central India. She became one of the best-known leaders of the revolt of 1857 against the British [[@east-india-company|East India Company]].

After her husband died in 1853, the Company refused to accept her adopted son as heir and took over Jhansi. She protested in writing for years. When the great uprising spread in 1857, Jhansi joined, and she took charge of its defence. In 1858 British forces stormed the city. She escaped, fought on with other rebel leaders and was killed in battle near Gwalior in June 1858. A British general who fought her praised her courage. In India she became a symbol of bravery and resistance.

st.reveal: Under the "Doctrine of Lapse", if a ruler died without a son by birth, the British could take the kingdom. Gangadhar Rao had adopted a boy just before he died, but Dalhousie refused to accept him as heir. Satara, Nagpur and Jhansi were all taken this way.

sec.t:
Lakshmibai was born Manikarnika Tambe, probably in 1828, in [[@varanasi|Varanasi]]. Her family called her Manu. Her mother died when she was small, and she grew up at the court of the Peshwa in exile at Bithoor, near Kanpur, where her father worked.

There, unusually for a girl of the time, she learned to ride, fence and shoot. Her childhood companions are said to have included Nana Sahib and Tatya Tope, who would later become leaders of the revolt too.

In May 1857, Indian soldiers rose up against the Company at Meerut, and the [[@revolt-1857|revolt]] spread across north India. In June, soldiers at Jhansi rebelled and killed British officers and their families. Historians still debate how much the Rani knew or controlled at that moment.

Afterwards she governed Jhansi, raised troops and strengthened its walls. In March 1858, a British force under Sir Hugh Rose besieged the city. For about two weeks the defenders fired back from the fort.

When Jhansi fell in April 1858, the Rani escaped at night on horseback, with her son, according to popular tradition, tied to her back. She joined Tatya Tope at Kalpi, and together they seized the great fort of Gwalior.

British forces soon attacked. On 17 or 18 June 1858, she was fatally wounded while fighting near Gwalior, dressed as a cavalry soldier. She was probably not yet 30. Her son survived and lived quietly for many years afterwards.

In the 1930s, the [[@hindi-language|Hindi]] poet Subhadra Kumari Chauhan wrote a stirring [[@poetry|poem]] about her. Its refrain says she fought bravely, and generations of Indian children have learned it by heart.

During the [[@world-war-two|Second World War]], [[@subhas-bose|Subhas Chandra Bose]] named the women's regiment of his army after her. Statues of the Rani on horseback, sword raised, stand in Jhansi, Gwalior and many other cities. Her fort at Jhansi is still there, high on a rocky hill, and visitors can see the spot from which, the story goes, she leapt on horseback to escape.

text: The Second World War was fought from 1939 to 1945 between two groups of countries. The Axis was led by [[@germany|Germany]], Italy and Japan. The Allies were led by Britain, the Soviet Union, the USA and China. It was fought across Europe, Asia, Africa and every ocean.

It was the deadliest conflict in history. Roughly 7 to 8.5 crore people died, more of them civilians than soldiers. The war ended with the defeat of Germany in May 1945 and Japan in August 1945. Afterwards, the world's map, its powerful countries and its ideas about keeping the peace all changed.

sec.t:
Many Germans were angry and poor after losing the [[@world-war-one|First World War]]. In 1933, Adolf Hitler and his Nazi party came to power. They blamed Jewish people and others for Germany's troubles, built up a huge army and began taking over neighbouring lands.

On 1 September 1939, Germany invaded Poland. Two days later, Britain and France declared war. By mid-1940 Germany had conquered much of western Europe, including France. Britain held out, and in 1941 Germany invaded the Soviet Union.

In Asia, Japan had been at war with China since 1937. In December 1941 it attacked the US base at Pearl Harbor, and the USA joined the war.

The Nazis set out to murder Europe's Jewish people. About 60 lakh Jewish men, women and children were killed, along with Roma people, disabled people and others. This is called the [[@holocaust|Holocaust]]. The diary of [[@anne-frank|Anne Frank]], a Jewish girl who hid with her family in Amsterdam, has helped millions of readers understand what was lost.

Codes and code-breaking mattered enormously. At Bletchley Park in England, thousands of people, many of them young women, worked to read German messages. [[@alan-turing|Alan Turing]] helped design machines to crack the German Enigma code. In the Pacific, US Marines used Navajo speakers to send messages the Japanese could not understand.

{{story:code-talkers}}

India was still ruled by Britain, and the British declared India at war without asking Indian leaders. Congress protested, and in 1942 launched the [[@quit-india|Quit India]] movement. Meanwhile, about 25 lakh Indians volunteered for the army and served in Africa, Italy and Southeast Asia.

In 1944 Japanese forces, with soldiers of [[@subhas-bose|Subhas Chandra Bose]]'s [[@indian-national-army|Indian National Army]], pushed into Manipur and Nagaland. At Imphal and Kohima in [[@northeast-india|northeast India]], Allied troops, most of them Indian, stopped them after months of fighting. Many Naga and Manipuri villagers helped carry supplies.

In 1943, a terrible [[famine|famine]] struck Bengal, and around 30 lakh people died. Historians agree that war, rising prices and government decisions made it far worse.

On 6 June 1944, D-Day, Allied soldiers landed on the beaches of Normandy in France. Soviet armies pushed in from the east. Germany surrendered on 8 May 1945.

Japan fought on. In August 1945 the USA dropped atomic bombs on the cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, killing many tens of thousands of people at once. Japan surrendered days later and signed the formal surrender on 2 September 1945.

The war left Europe and much of Asia in ruins. In 1945, countries founded the [[@united-nations|United Nations]] to try to stop such a war happening again. The USA and the Soviet Union came out as the two most powerful nations, and soon became rivals in the [[@cold-war|Cold War]].

Britain was exhausted, and its [[empire|empire]] began to end. Two years later, in 1947, India became independent. At Kohima, a war cemetery stands on the hill where the tennis court once was.

text: The smallest country in the world is Vatican City, inside the city of Rome in Italy. It covers about 0.44 square kilometres, less than many university campuses. Next comes Monaco, on the coast of France, at about 2 square km. Then come three island countries in the Pacific and Europe's hilltop [[republic|republic]] of San Marino.
India is about 7 million times bigger than the Vatican. But tiny countries still have flags, laws, stamps and sometimes even their own football teams.

d.try: Find a map of your own town or city and look up the area of your neighbourhood, a big park or your school campus. Compare it with Vatican City (0.44 sq km) and Monaco (2 sq km). You may find that something near you is bigger than a whole country.
myth: A tiny place can't really be a full country.

Size doesn't decide it. Vatican City, Monaco, Nauru and Tuvalu all run their own affairs and are recognised by other countries. All except the Vatican are full members of the United Nations, and the Vatican takes part as an observer.

sec.h: Vatican City: a country inside a city
sec.t:
Vatican City is the home of the Pope, the head of the Roman Catholic Church. It became an independent country in 1929 through a [[treaty|treaty]] with Italy. Its walls enclose St Peter's Basilica, the Vatican Museums and gardens.

Fewer than 1,000 people live there. Most are priests, nuns and the Swiss Guards, who have protected the Pope since 1506 in their striped uniforms. Almost nobody is born there. Citizenship usually comes with a job, and ends when the job does.

Yet it has a post office, a radio station, a railway station with very short track, its own stamps and coins, and a pharmacy. Millions of tourists visit every year, far outnumbering the residents.

Nauru is a single oval island in the Pacific, about 21 square km. You could drive right around it in about half an hour. It has no official capital city.

For much of the 20th century, Nauru was rich from mining phosphate, a mineral made from ancient seabird droppings that farmers use as [[fertiliser|fertiliser]]. Mining stripped much of the island's centre, leaving jagged limestone pinnacles. Most of its roughly 12,000 people live along the coast.

sec.h: Tuvalu: a country barely above water
sec.t:
Tuvalu is made of nine small islands and [[atoll|atolls]], adding up to about 26 square km. Its highest point is only about 4.6 metres above sea level.

That makes it one of the countries most at risk from [[@sea-level-rise|rising seas]]. In 2023, Tuvalu signed a treaty with Australia allowing some of its citizens to move there each year. Tuvalu has also started making a digital copy of the country online, so its history and culture are saved even if land is lost.

San Marino, on a mountain inside Italy, covers about 61 square km. It claims to be the oldest surviving republic in the world, founded, by tradition, in the year 301.

Next come Liechtenstein, between Switzerland and Austria, the Marshall Islands and Saint Kitts and Nevis. In Asia, the smallest country is the [[@maldives|Maldives]], with about 1,200 coral islands adding up to roughly 300 square km.

Being small has advantages. Tiny countries can be fast at making decisions, and some, like Monaco and Liechtenstein, are wealthy. But they can't easily grow food or defend themselves, so they rely on friendly neighbours.

And there are bigger surprises in the opposite direction. Some cities, like Tokyo or Delhi, hold more people than whole countries, as you'll find among the [[@extreme-biggest-cities|world's biggest cities]]. Delhi alone has hundreds of times more people than Monaco, Nauru, Tuvalu and San Marino put together.

text: NASA, the US space agency, does its work at ten main centres spread across the country, plus its headquarters in Washington, DC. Each has a specialty. Some build rockets, some test engines, some train astronauts, some study Earth's [[climate|climate]], and one drives robots on Mars.

The two most famous are Kennedy Space Center in Florida, where astronauts blast off, and Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas, where they train and where Mission Control watches over them. In April 2026 both were busy with Artemis II, which carried four astronauts around the Moon and back in about ten days, the first crew to go that far since 1972.

st.prompt: A rocket with astronauts lifts off from Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Once it clears the launch tower, who takes charge of the mission?

options.t: Mission Control in Houston, Texas
The launch team in Florida, all the way to space
NASA headquarters in Washington, DC

st.reveal: The Florida team handles the countdown and liftoff. As soon as the rocket clears the tower, flight controllers at Johnson Space Center in Houston take over and stay with the crew for the rest of the mission.

src: NASA, NASA centers and facilities.
NASA, Artemis II mission overview (2026).
