d.try: Make a "mission control" with family or friends. One person is the astronaut and sits behind a sofa, out of sight, building a simple block tower. The others sit at a table and give spoken instructions from a picture of the finished tower. Swap roles and see how clear the instructions need to be.
myth: NASA does all its work at one big space centre.
NASA is spread across ten main centres in different states, each with its own job, from testing rocket engines in Mississippi to studying aircraft in California.
facts: run from the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California
launched 1 April 2026, flew four astronauts around the Moon

sec.t:
Kennedy sits on the Atlantic coast, next to the US Space Force base at Cape Canaveral. Launching east over the ocean is safer, because falling rocket parts land in water, and Earth's spin gives a free push. That's why most [[@launch-sites|launch sites]] are near a coast.

Its giant Vehicle Assembly Building was built for the Saturn V Moon rockets. It is so tall that its doors, about 139 m high, are among the largest in the world. Launch Complex 39A, where Apollo 11 lifted off, is still used today. Visitors can tour the site and stand under a real Saturn V lying on its side.

In Pasadena, California, the Jet Propulsion Laboratory builds and drives robotic spacecraft. It is run for NASA by the Caltech university. Engineers there sent the Voyager probes past the outer planets and now operate the [[@mars-rovers|Mars rovers]], including Curiosity and Perseverance.

Because radio signals take several minutes to reach Mars, nobody can steer a [[rover|rover]] with a joystick. Drivers plan each day's moves in advance and send them up as a list of commands.

NASA also works with private companies and other countries. SpaceX rockets carry astronauts to the space station from Launch Complex 39A, which NASA leases to the company. In 2025 a radar satellite called NISAR, built jointly by NASA and India's space agency, launched from Sriharikota to map changes on Earth's surface. It was one of the biggest joint projects in NASA's links with [[@isro-missions|ISRO]].

Marshall Space Flight Center in Alabama designed the Saturn V and now the Space Launch System rocket used for Artemis. Stennis in Mississippi fires rocket engines on giant test stands that shake the ground for kilometres. Goddard in Maryland builds Earth-watching satellites and helps run the Hubble and Webb space telescopes.

Langley in Virginia, the oldest centre, began in 1917 as an aircraft lab. In the 1950s and 1960s, women mathematicians there, including Katherine Johnson, worked out spacecraft paths by hand. Glenn in Ohio works on engines and power. Ames and Armstrong, both in California, study aircraft and supercomputing. Together they show that sending one person to space takes thousands of people on the ground, most of whom never leave Earth.

text: Akbar was one of the greatest Mughal emperors. He ruled much of north and central India from 1556 to 1605. Birbal was one of his courtiers, a Hindu poet and musician who became a close friend and adviser.

In the stories, Akbar asks tricky questions or sets strange tests, and Birbal always finds a smart way out. Jealous courtiers try to trap him and fail. The king gets puzzled, then laughs. These tales are still told across India and Pakistan in homes, schoolbooks, comics and cartoons.

st.prompt: Akbar asked how many crows lived in his city. What did Birbal do?

options.t: Gave a number, with a clever excuse ready if anyone counted differently
Sent soldiers to count every crow
Said it was impossible to know

st.reveal: Birbal named a number at once. If there were more crows, he said, some had come to visit relatives. If there were fewer, some had gone away to visit theirs. The king laughed, and nobody could prove him wrong.

src: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Akbar.
Abul Fazl, Akbarnama (the official history of Akbar's reign).
n.certNote: Akbar and Birbal were real people, and Birbal really was close to the emperor. But almost all the funny stories about them were told and retold long after both had died, so historians treat them as folk tales.

d.try: Write your own Birbal story. Think of an impossible question a king might ask, such as how many stars are in the sky. Then find an answer that is cheeky, quick and impossible to disprove, and try it out on your family.
myth: Birbal is a made-up character, like a fairy-tale hero.

Birbal was a real man at Akbar's court, and the emperor gave him the title of Raja. What is made up is most of the stories. They were added over centuries by storytellers who loved the idea of a clever adviser.
facts: folk tale and battle of wits

sec.h: The real men behind the tales
sec.t:
[[@akbar|Akbar]] became emperor at just thirteen. He grew curious about many faiths and invited scholars of different religions to debate at his court. He also built a red sandstone city called Fatehpur Sikri, near Agra.

Birbal was born in a Brahmin family, and his birth name is often given as Mahesh Das. He wrote poems in Braj Bhasha, a form of [[@hindi-language|Hindi]], and Akbar gave him the titles Birbal and Raja. In 1586, Birbal was sent with an army into the mountains of the north-west, near the Swat valley. He was killed there in an ambush. Court records say Akbar grieved for him deeply.

Later tradition counts Birbal among Akbar's "nine jewels", or navaratnas, along with the singer Tansen, the finance minister Todar Mal and the historian Abul Fazl. These were all real people at the court. Historians doubt there was ever an official club of exactly nine, but the idea shows how famous the court's talent became.

After Birbal died, people kept telling stories about him. New ones were added, and old jokes from elsewhere were given his name. Some of the same plots turn up in tales of [[@tenali-raman|Tenali Raman]] in the south, and in stories of Mulla Nasruddin from Turkey to Central Asia. A good trick travels.

The tales usually follow a pattern. A powerful person is about to do something unfair or silly. A clever person shows them the mistake without saying it directly. That lets listeners enjoy a small, safe kind of rebellion: brains beating rank.

sec.h: From the court to the comic book
sec.t:
In the twentieth century the stories moved into print. [[@amar-chitra-katha|Amar Chitra Katha]] published Birbal comics that many Indian children read before they could spell "Mughal". [[@television-invented|Television]] shows and cartoons followed.

Today a house at Fatehpur Sikri is still called Birbal's Palace. Historians aren't sure he ever lived in it, which suits him. Like the stories, the name sticks because people want it to be true. The real history of the [[@mughals|Mughals]] is full of wars and politics. The Birbal stories keep a lighter memory of the same court, where a joke could sometimes win an argument.

text: Gulab jamun is a soft ball of milk dough, fried until golden brown and soaked in sugar syrup. Its roots probably lie outside India. Food historians think it grew from fried dough balls soaked in honey or syrup that were eaten in Persia and the Arab world for centuries.

When such ideas reached India, cooks made them their own, using *khoya*, milk boiled down for hours until it turns thick and fudgy. The name says a lot. *Gulab* comes from Persian words meaning rosewater, often used to scent the syrup. *Jamun* is the dark purple Indian fruit that the finished sweets resemble.

st.prompt: Why are gulab jamuns fried slowly over low heat instead of in very hot oil?

options.t: So the inside cooks through before the outside burns
So they stay white
Because hot oil would melt the sugar

st.reveal: The dough is thick and dense. In very hot oil, the outside turns dark brown while the middle stays raw and doughy. Slow frying lets heat reach the centre, so the balls swell and can soak up syrup evenly.

src: Achaya K.T. (1998) A Historical Dictionary of Indian Food. Oxford University Press.
Davidson A. (2014) The Oxford Companion to Food. Oxford University Press.
n.certNote: Food historians agree gulab jamun is related to fried dough balls in syrup from Persia and the Arab world. Exactly when and where it took its Indian form is unknown, and popular stories about a royal Mughal cook are not proven.

d.try: Mix a few spoons of sugar into a cup of room-temperature water until it dissolves. Drop in a cube of sponge cake or a piece of rusk, and watch it soak up the liquid and swell. That is what a fried gulab jamun does in syrup.
myth: Gulab jamun is made with roses and jamun fruit.
Neither is in it. "Gulab" comes from the rosewater often added to the syrup, and "jamun" refers to the fruit it looks like, small, round and dark.
facts: Persian gol (flower) plus ab (water), meaning rosewater, plus jamun, a dark purple fruit
khoya, milk boiled down until thick
luqmat al-qadi from the Arab world, Bengal's pantua and ledikeni
fried slowly, then soaked in warm sugar syrup

sec.t:
In the Arab world, cooks have long made *luqmat al-qadi*, which means "the judge's morsels". These are small fried balls of [[yeast|yeast]] dough, drenched in honey or syrup. They appear in cookbooks from Baghdad written around 800 years ago. Persians made similar sweets.

Persian-speaking traders, soldiers and rulers brought many foods and words to India. Under the Delhi Sultanate and later the [[@mughals|Mughals]], Persian was the language of royal courts. It is likely that the idea of a fried, syrup-soaked ball met Indian milk sweets somewhere along the way. A popular story says a cook of Emperor Shah Jahan invented gulab jamun by accident. It is a fun tale, but there is no written proof.

India has a whole family of gulab jamun relatives. *Kala jamun* is fried longer until it is almost black. Bengal has *pantua*, made partly with chhena, a fresh cheese. One famous Bengal version is called *ledikeni*. The story goes that a Kolkata sweet maker created it in the 1850s to honour Lady Canning, the wife of the governor-general, and people mispronounced her name.

In Rajasthan, some cooks go further. *Gulab jamun ki sabzi* is a curry where the sweets go into a spicy tomato and onion gravy, so every bite is sweet, salty and hot together. It sounds strange, but plenty of Rajasthani families swear by it, and cooking videos of it get curious viewers from all over India.

Gulab jamun turns up at weddings, birthdays and festivals like Diwali and Eid. Shops in India sell it from huge steel pots, and tins of it are shipped to Indian grocery stores across the USA, the UK and the Gulf.

It is very sweet, and a single gulab jamun can carry about as much [[@sugar|sugar]] as two or three teaspoons, so most families save it for special days. The same syrup trick appears in another favourite, the crunchy spiral [[@food-jalebi|jalebi]], which also has cousins across the Middle East. And at the heart of both lies one of India's oldest skills, turning plain [[@milk|milk]] into dozens of sweets.

text: Jaggery, called gur in Hindi, is a traditional sweetener made by boiling sugarcane juice until it turns thick, sticky and golden-brown. It is then poured into moulds and left to set into blocks or cones. In some regions, especially Bengal and Tamil Nadu, jaggery is also made from the sap of date or palmyra palms.

Unlike white sugar, jaggery isn't refined. It keeps the brown [[@oddity-great-molasses-flood|molasses]] and a little of the minerals from the cane. That gives it a rich, caramel-like taste. India makes most of the world's jaggery and uses it in [[@candy-history|sweets]], dals, drinks and [[@festival-foods|festival foods]].

st.prompt: Jaggery is brown, while white sugar is white. What makes the difference?

options.t: Jaggery keeps the molasses that white sugar has removed
Jaggery is made from a different, brown kind of sugarcane
Jaggery is burnt sugar

st.reveal: Jaggery is simply cane juice boiled down until it sets, so it keeps the dark, sticky molasses and small amounts of minerals. To make white sugar, factories spin and wash out the molasses, leaving pure white crystals.

src: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), information on non-centrifugal sugar.
Achaya K. T., Indian Food, A Historical Companion, Oxford University Press, 1994.
Britannica, Jaggery; Sugar.

d.try: Do a taste-and-dissolve test with an adult. Put a small piece of jaggery in one cup of warm water and a spoon of white sugar in another. Stir both and compare how fast they dissolve and what colour the water turns. Then taste a tiny bit of each and describe the difference.
myth: Jaggery is healthy, so you can eat as much as you like, unlike sugar.
Jaggery has small amounts of iron and other minerals, but it is still mostly sugar. Eaten in large amounts, it affects teeth and health much like white sugar does.
facts: sugarcane juice, or the sap of date and palmyra palms
juice boiled in big open pans until thick, then set in moulds

sec.t:
In the winter harvest season, sugarcane is cut and taken to small workshops called kolhus or gur-making units. There, crushers squeeze out the juice.

The juice is poured into huge, shallow iron pans over a fire. As it [[@boiling-water|boils]], water evaporates and the juice thickens. Workers skim off the scum that rises to the top, sometimes adding plant extracts to help clean it. After a few hours, the thick, golden liquid is stirred, cooled and poured into moulds.

The whole process is simple and has changed little in centuries, though many units now use better furnaces. Kolhapur in Maharashtra is especially famous for its jaggery, and its market yard trades huge amounts every season.

In Bengal, a special winter jaggery called nolen gur is made from the sap of date palms. Tappers climb the trees in the cold early morning to collect the sap. Nolen gur has a smoky, fragrant taste and goes into Bengali sweets like sandesh and [[@bengali-food|rosogolla]].

In Tamil Nadu and Kerala, palmyra palms give karupatti, a darker palm jaggery with a deep, earthy flavour.

Jaggery is part of many celebrations. On Makar Sankranti in Maharashtra, people exchange tilgul, sweets made of sesame seeds and jaggery. In Tamil Nadu, sweet pongal is made with new rice, moong dal and jaggery during the harvest festival of [[@onam-pongal|Pongal]].

Chikki, a crunchy sweet of [[@peanut-butter|peanuts]] and jaggery, is famous in Lonavala in Maharashtra. Many families also add a small piece of jaggery to dal, especially in Gujarat and Maharashtra, for a sweet-sour taste.

Many people think jaggery is much healthier than white sugar. It does contain small amounts of iron, potassium and magnesium, which white sugar lacks. But it's still around 80 per cent or more sugar.

Too much of any sugar can cause [[@tooth-decay|tooth decay]] and other health problems. The [[bacteria|bacteria]] in your mouth don't care whether the [[@sugar-teeth|sugar]] came from a factory or a village pan. Jaggery's taste and traditions are good reasons to enjoy it, but it's still a treat, not a health food. Sweet things, in any form, are best eaten in small amounts.
